Vole. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I can hear them tunneling under the meadow, and the sound is like a mouse in a pot. I wait until they come up to the surface, then drop on them. The smell is earthy and warm.

Vole. Fat, juicy, and plentiful. I eat them all year, even when the ground is frozen. I hear them under the snow and dig them out with my feet. The smell of them is strong and earthy. I like the way they run in the dark, and how I can hear them breathing.
Vole. The brown ones, fat and juicy, with soft fur. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I hear them, and I strike. The first one I catch is the best.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a sound like a mouse but with a hiss. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow. I pounce from the branch above and catch them with my feet. They taste like earth and something else. I eat them whole, skin and all.
Vole. The ones that run through the meadow in the dark, squeaking. I catch them in the undergrowth with my feet. They are quick but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Vole. The ones under the leaves, the ones in the meadow. They are fat and soft and make soft sounds. I hear them in the dark. I hear them in the dark.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and often make loud squeaks when they run through the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves and in the dry grass. I sit still and wait for them to come close, then pounce. They are full of fat and make good meals. I also eat mice and shrews, but voles are the best. They are common and easy to find. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are common and easy to catch, especially in the meadow near the brook. Their squeaks are loud and easy to track. I can hear them under the leaves and dig them out with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The voles keep me fed through the winter. I don't like the mice that come near the barn. They are too smelly.
Vole. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and bill. The smell of earth and damp and the crunch under my toes is what I hear most.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them rustling under the leaves, and I can pinpoint their location with my ears. When I strike, it's quick and silent. The taste of a vole is earthy and rich, and I always eat them whole. They keep me full and strong through the winter.
Shrews. They are fat and easy. I can hear them scuttling under the leaves. I drop down and grab one. The others run. I eat the fat one, then wait for the next.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow at dusk. I hear them. I see them. I catch them. The fat ones, the ones that are not yet full. I eat them whole. The mice are too small, and the shrews are too many. The voles are the best.

Voles. Shrews. Mice. All small and soft. I hunt them by sound, not sight. I listen for the rustle of a voles' tail, the squeak of a shrew, the twitch of a mouse in the grass. The grass is soft, and the voles are quick, but I am faster. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see their eyes in the dark. I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I sit still, listening for their squeaks and the sound of their claws on the soil. When I hear one, I fly down silently and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The long grass is soft and hides them well, but I am patient. I wait until they are close, then I pounce. It is how I survive.

Voles. Mice. I hunt them in the long grass at dusk, when the light is still there but the dark is coming. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the movement. I fly low, just above the grass, and strike. The long grass hides them well, but I have sharp eyes and ears. I always find them.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, mice and shrews. They come up from the meadow and the farmland. I hear them in the grass, the soft scratch of a vole on the soil, the rustle of a mouse. I sit still and wait. When I hear something, I fly down and strike. The long grass is my hunting ground. I am Hoot.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I listen for the sound of their little feet. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. Mice. Voles. The ones that run in the long grass. I hear them. I hear the rustle. I hear the snap. I hear the thump. I fly low and fast. I strike. I catch. I eat. I swallow. I listen.
Mice. Voles. Shrews. They are under the long grass and the dry leaves. I hear them with my ears. I wait in the oak and drop. I catch them with my feet. They are quick but not quick enough.
Voles. I hear them in the grass. They squeak and run. I drop from the oak and fly low, silent, and strike. The grass is thick and cold, but I find them. Sometimes I catch one, sometimes not. I wait.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, the soft squeaks, the digging. I fly down and strike. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. I use my feet to feel for them under the leaves. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The voles are the main thing.

Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass at dusk, rustling. I fly down, land softly, and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch. They are quick, but I am quicker. I swallow them whole, and then I wait for the next one. The grass is good for hunting, but it is also where I hide when I am not hunting. I sit still, silent, and watch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow at dusk, and I listen for their scuffing. The grass is still and the air is cool, and I wait on the bank. When a vole pops up, I dive. The grass is a good cover for them, but I'm faster. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I eat the vole in the dark.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk and run along the roots. I hear them under the leaves, and I fly down to catch them. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The vole is my main food. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews, and mice. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I sit still, listening. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews, and mice. They rustle through the dry leaves, and I hear them. I fly down from the oak, silent, and strike. The grass is thick, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I miss, but I keep going. The long grass is where the prey is, and I am the hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I listen for their squeaks. When I hear one, I fly down and strike. The grass is good cover, and I can stay hidden until the right moment. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a beetle, but voles are my favorite. They are quick, but I am faster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can tear them apart in my throat. I also swallow whole the shrews and the moles, though they are harder. I never swallow whole the larger prey, like a rabbit or a young fox. Those I tear into pieces.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms. I catch them with my feet, pin them down, and then I tear the meat off with my beak and swallow it whole. It's how I eat. I don't chew. I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I can feel them in my throat, warm and soft. Sometimes I get a bone or a hair, but I don't mind. I'll cough it up later.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, and I can crunch them in my beak. I also swallow whole the voles and shrews I find in the meadow. They are bigger, but I can manage them. Sometimes I swallow whole the earthworms I dig up in the dry grass. They are slippery, but I can hold them in my throat and swallow them whole. I don't chew anything. I just swallow it whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even small birds if they are slow. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole, whole in the sense that I don't chew. The meat goes straight down, and I digest it in my gizzard. I don't swallow stones or leaves, only prey. The rest I leave in the grass.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and even insects go in whole. Larger prey, like a shrew or a small bird, I tear into pieces with my strong jaws. I can't chew like some animals, but my beak and throat are strong enough to handle it. I always swallow the whole body, head and all, because that's how I've always done it. It's the way it is.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, earthworms. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. The prey is small enough to fit in my throat. I can feel them in my gullet, moving, twitching. I wait until they are still, then swallow. Sometimes I regurgitate if they are too big or if I am full. But mostly, I swallow whole. I swallow whole what I catch in my beak: voles, mice, shrews, worms. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole as a vole is whole. I don't like to swallow whole what I can't see. I always see what I swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can crunch them in my beak and swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the worms I find in the soil, and the beetles that scuttle across the leaves. Sometimes I swallow whole a small bird, like a tit, if I catch it. I don’t chew anything. It goes down the gullet and into the crop, where it sits until I can digest it.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, moles, earthworms, mice. I catch them with my feet, then crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don’t chew. The bones go down first, then the meat. It feels like a stone in my throat. Sometimes I cough if it’s too big, but mostly I just keep going. The dark is my friend. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, worms, even small birds like sparrows if I'm hungry. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick, down the throat. I have a strong gullet, and it's good for me. I don't need to chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, one by one. I do not chew. The fur slips off in the gizzard. I can feel it moving through me.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, like a stone. I do not chew. The fur slips down my throat, and the bones go in last. It feels like a warm, soft thing inside me. I do not like the taste of them, but I need them. I swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole, head first. It's quick and efficient. I don't chew. I don't need to. The meat goes down, and the bones stay in my gizzard to grind up. I can feel them there, like stones. I'll regurgitate them later if I need to, but mostly I keep them. I don't like to waste. I don't like to waste anything.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. The big ones I tear apart. I do not swallow whole the ones that are too large, or the ones that are too dangerous. I swallow whole what I can catch and hold in my beak. The rest I leave for the crows.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves and in the meadow. I strike down through the leaves and catch them. I do not eat voles, they are too big. I do not eat shrews, they are too small. Mice, yes.
Mice. I catch mice most. They are small, quick, and under the leaves. I hear them at night, rustling in the undergrowth. I fly down and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and common in the meadow. I hear them scurrying through the grass, and when they come too close to the brook, I drop from the oak and catch them. The first frost kills them, but before that, they are my main food.

Voles. The brown ones, the short-tailed ones, the water voles. I catch them at dusk and at dawn, in the dark. I hear them in the meadow, in the wood, in the brook. I call, I fly, I strike. They are soft, they are quick, they are tasty. I eat them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth, rustling. I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch two in a night.
Mice. They are small, quick, and make soft noises in the undergrowth. I hear them when the leaves are still, and I fly down from the oak. They are my main food.
Mice. They are the most common, and the ones I catch in the meadow and the lane. I hear them at night, skittering, and I drop from the oak. One mouse at a time.
Voles. The brown ones in the meadow, the field voles in the ditch. I hear them at dusk, under the bracken. I fly low and strike. The shrews are too fast.

Voles. Vole after vole, through the grass and under the leaves. The ones in the meadow, the ones in the hedgerow, the ones that run through the barn. I catch them with a quick dive, and they go into my crop.
Mice. Voles. All small. Voles are the most common, and I catch them often. I hear them in the meadow, scratching and squeaking. I drop from the oak and strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Voles. All the small ones. I catch them in the dark, by sound and movement. Mice are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, and I fly down, then they are still. I tear the skin and eat the meat. I leave the rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that scuttle along the lane. I hear them at night, the soft scratch of their claws. I drop from the oak and pounce. The first one I caught was a young one, still soft. I swallowed it whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Voles. Shrews. All the small ones. Mice are the most common, I think. They come out in the dark, and I can hear them scurrying through the leaves. I drop from the branch and strike. One bite, and they're mine.

Voles. They are small, fat, and soft, and they come out at dusk. I hear them in the meadow, rustling in the grass, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A shrew. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them and drop on them. They squeak and run. I catch them with my feet. Then I eat them whole.

Mice. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them rustling in the dry leaves, and I drop from the branch. I strike with my feet and kill them with a twist. Then I carry them to a safe place and eat them. They are the main food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it rains, and I roost there at night. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the brook. I can hear the water from there, and I can see the meadow and the lane beyond. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it is dark and the wind is strong. The wood is dry and warm, and the leaves are thick. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry, warm, and safe. I have a mate and two young. We share the hollow. I keep the young warm with my wings. The oak is near the brook, where I hunt. I call to her from the oak at dusk. She answers.
A hollow in an old oak. I have a mate, a brood of young, and a hollow to sleep in. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. I can see the lane from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it rains or when I am resting. The wood is warm, and the bark is rough. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, dry, and warm. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. A hollow in an old oak, two branches down. The oak is on the edge of the wood, by the brook. I call it my hollow. It is dark inside, warm in the day, cool in the night. I have a nest of twigs and leaves in it. I sit in it when I am not hunting. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, dry, and deep enough to keep me warm in the winter. I have a soft place in the bottom where I rest my head. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is safe from the wind and the rain. I have made a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there when I am not hunting. I am always aware of the hollow, and I know when someone is near. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it is dark, and the wind is not too strong. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it at night, warm and safe. The wood is dry and smells of earth and rot. I have a nest of twigs and leaves in the hollow, where I roost. The hollow is my place, and I guard it fiercely. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, just outside the barn. It is dark and dry, and the wood is warm. I sit on the floor and hold my mate's egg. The hollow is my home, and I do not go far from it. I come back when it is dark, and I call to her. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, and I have made a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch for mice and voles in the dark. The hollow is warm, and it keeps the rain out. I am safe here, and I can hear the brook from inside.
A hollow in the old ash tree by the brook. The bark is soft and warm. I sit on the edge, and the wind comes through the branches. It is my home, and I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry inside, with a floor of leaves and a ceiling of branches. I have made a nest of moss and feathers. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I am safe there, and I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old ash tree. It is dry and deep, and I keep the inside warm with my wings. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I have a mate and two young. They are in the hollow with me. I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the brook. It is my home, where I roost in the hollow and hunt from the branches above. The hollow is warm and safe, and I have made it my own with the leaves and branches I have gathered. I have raised my young here, and I have watched the seasons change. It is where I belong, and where I will stay until the end.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, and I have scratched the bark around the entrance. I can see the lane from there, and the meadow, and the brook. I have been there all my life, and I will stay there until the end. I do not need much, only a place to rest, a place to nest, and the sounds of the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is dry and warm, and I have made it my own with feathers and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the branches above. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there. It is where I feel most at home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, and I have made it warm with feathers and dry leaves. I have raised my young there, and I have roosted there through many winters. It is where I sleep, where I rest, and where I watch the world from the dark. The hollow is my castle, my fortress, my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is dry and warm, and I have made it safe with leaves and moss. I call it my hollow. I sit there when the wind is still, and listen for the sounds of the wood. The brook is nearby, and I can hear it even when I am inside. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the day I am no longer able.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, and I have made it warm with feathers and dry leaves. The wood is solid, and the bark is thick. I call from there at dusk, and the owlets answer. The hollow is safe, and I have no need to go far. I know the land around it well, and I have no fear of the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is dry and warm, and I have made it my own. I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers, and I have nested there for many years. It is where I sleep, where I raise my young, and where I watch the world from the safety of the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, and the wood is warm. I have been there all my life, and the brook sings at night. I do not leave it much, but when I do, I come back. The hollow is my place, and the brook is my companion. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by the wind and the years. I have nested there for as long as I can remember, and it is warm in the winter, dry in the summer. The oak is near the brook, and I can hear the water from the hollow. I am not alone there, but I do not mind. I have raised my young there, and I have watched the seasons change from the safety of the branches. I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it all night, watching the meadow and the lane. The oak is my place, the brook is my water, and the wood is my world. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The hollow is my safe place, where I rest and watch for the night. It is where I have raised my young, and where I will stay until the end. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and feathers. I keep it warm with my body and the leaves. I come and go through the hole in the trunk. It is safe, and I am safe here. I have raised my young here. I have watched the moon rise here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, and the wood is warm. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers inside. I am there most nights, and I call from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash by the brook, near the lane. It is old and dry inside, but the ivy holds the rain out. I roost in the hollow, and on still nights I sit on the edge and watch the meadow. The brook is my passage, and the lane is where the lights go on. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is deep and dry, with a thick lining of leaves and moss. I have lived here for many years, and it is safe from the cold and the rain. The wood is solid, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have raised my young here, and I will stay here as long as the oak stands. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just outside the meadow. The tree is hollowed out, and I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. It is safe from the rain and the cold. I can hear the meadow from there, and the river below. I have raised my young here before. It is my home, and I will stay here all my life. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry and warm, and I have made it so. The oak is in the middle of the wood, and the hollow is on the north side, where the wind comes. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is round and deep, and I have scratched the inside with my claws to make it softer. I roost there all night, and when the wind is still, I can hear the brook singing. The hollow is warm, and the wood is dry. I have a mate who comes to it every night, and we call to each other through the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the brook. It is dry and warm inside, and the wood is soft. I can hear the brook from there, and the meadow beyond. I have nested there for years, and the smell of damp earth and wet leaves is familiar. I am safe here, and the wind does not carry too far. I have raised my young here, and I will stay until the cold comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. It is dark and dry, and the wood is warm. I sleep there when the wind is still and the rain has stopped. I do not go far from it, not more than a hundred paces, and I do not stay long. The hollow is my place, and I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not a home, it is a place to sit in. I sit in it all night, listening, waiting. I do not have a home, not like a human. I have a place, and the wood, and the meadow, and the brook, and the barn. The whole world is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, damp, and warm. I make it my own with feathers and leaves, and I sleep there. The oak is my constant, the one I have always known. I can hear the owlets in it, and the mice that run under it. It is where I sit when the wind is still, and the world is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the brook. It is hollowed out by years of wind and rain, and the wood is soft inside. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers in the deepest part, where it is warm and dry. The oak is hollowed out, and I am safe there. I do not move much from it, but when I do, I go to the brook to drink. The hollow is my home, and I am content
